analysis.one_liner: Caps insulin copays at $35 or less per 30-day supply and waives the deductible for insulin in employer and individual health plans.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 11 cosponsors including 3 Republicans, has sat with three House committees since its September 2, 2026 referral and no markup or floor vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require most health insurance plans, including employer plans, marketplace plans, and even bare-bones catastrophic plans, to cover at least one insulin of every type and delivery form with no deductible, no prior-authorization hoops, and copays capped at $35 per 30-day supply — or less, since after 2028 the cap is the lower of $35 or 25% of the insulin's negotiated net price after rebates. It would also speed up FDA review of biosimilar insulins when fewer than three compete with a brand-name product, run a government study of uninsured insulin users, and fund a $2-million-a-year resource center and 24/7 hotline to help uninsured people find discounted insulin.
analysis.who_benefits: People with diabetes who use insulin and have health insurance: they would pay no deductible and no more than $35 (often less) for a 30-day supply of a covered insulin of each type and delivery form, and could not be made to jump through prior-authorization steps to get it [S2]. Uninsured insulin users would get a federally funded resource center and 24/7 hotline to connect them with manufacturer assistance programs, community health centers, and enrollment help [S2]. Patients generally gain from faster review of competing biosimilar insulins, which tend to cost less than the brand originals [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Group health plans and insurers offering individual coverage must cover selected insulin products of every dosage form and delivery device (vial, pen, inhaler) and every insulin type, applying no deductible and capping cost-sharing at $35 per 30-day supply — or, for plan years starting 2028 or later, the lesser of $35 or 25% of the insulin's negotiated net price after all rebates, including those captured by pharmacy benefit managers [S2].
Plans may not impose prior authorization, medical management, or similar conditions on selected insulin products except when clinically justified for safety or reasonable quantity limits [S2].

Catastrophic health plans, which normally cover little before a very high out-of-pocket threshold, would have to cover selected insulin products on the same capped-cost terms before the deductible is met [S2].

The FDA could designate and expedite review of biosimilar insulin applications where a brand-name insulin has fewer than three biosimilar competitors and all exclusivity periods expired at least three years earlier, a pathway intended to bring more lower-priced copies to market [S2].

HHS would award a grant (authorized at $2 million per year for fiscal 2027-2032) for a resource center and 24/7 hotline that helps uninsured people enroll in manufacturer and other assistance programs, with conflict-of-interest standards barring insulin manufacturers from running it or paying for enrollment [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer health plans would absorb the cost of covering insulin without deductible and with capped copays, a cost that would flow partly into premiums; pharmacy benefit managers would lose some of the rebate and fee revenue the bill now counts against the copay cap and limits payments to; brand-name insulin makers would face a faster lane for biosimilar competitors on products with little competition [S2]. Taxpayers would fund the uninsured-assistance program and the GAO study [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers, PBMs, and brand-name drugmakers

drawbacks.text: The cost-sharing cap does not lower insulin list or net prices directly; it shifts the remaining cost to plans and employers, which typically shows up in premiums — so sicker patients save while everyone with coverage shares a bit of the cost [S2].

The bill does nothing to get insurance to uninsured people, who face the steepest insulin prices; for them it offers only a study and a $2-million-a-year hotline and referral service, not coverage [S2].

Plans only have to cover one 'selected' insulin of each type and form, and can impose higher cost-sharing on any insulin that is not a selected product or is filled out-of-network, so a patient whose doctor prescribes a non-selected brand could still face full cost-sharing [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For insured people who use insulin, the math is strongly favorable: a $35-or-less guaranteed copay with no deductible and no prior authorization removes the most common ways patients get stuck paying hundreds of dollars at the pharmacy counter. The real costs are absorbed by plans and employers and passed partly into premiums, and the bill leaves the underlying prices set by manufacturers largely untouched, betting instead that biosimilar competition will push them down over time. Its weakest point is the uninsured, who get help finding discounts but no coverage.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to three House committees on September 2, 2026, and none of the three has taken it up, so it sits awaiting action while the session runs toward its January 2027 end [S4].

narrative.text: Representative Diana DeGette introduced the bill on September 2, 2026, joined at introduction by Representatives Miller-Meeks, Schrier, Bresnahan, and Craig — a mix of Democrats and Republicans [S2].

It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the Ways and Means and Education and Workforce Committees; under House rules, a bill referred to multiple committees can be claimed by any of them, which means any one chair can keep it from advancing [S4].
No committee has scheduled a markup and no vote has occurred since the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far no final winner: the bill has not advanced, so health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers keep today's cost-sharing and rebate arrangements, and insulin users keep paying whatever their plans charge.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and PBMs, so far, by default

sides.party_line_note: No one has voted against it — there has been no vote — but sponsorship is bipartisan: 8 of the 11 cosponsors are Democrats and 3 are Republicans, and the bill's five original sponsors included two Republicans [S3].

industries.note: The copay cap is calculated after subtracting every price concession, including those captured by PBMs, and plans are barred from paying a PBM more than the capped amount for selected insulins — provisions aimed at stopping middlemen from pocketing insulin rebates. That rebate take is a core PBM revenue stream on a top-selling drug category [S2].

Insurers must cover selected insulins with no deductible, capped copays, and no prior authorization — new mandated coverage costs that flow into premiums — though the bill exempts the added insulin coverage from actuarial-value calculations. Their interest in keeping cost-sharing and prior-authorization practices runs against the patient savings the bill creates [S2].

The bill does not directly cap what manufacturers charge; the patient copay cap is borne by plans. But the biosimilar fast-track targets exactly their products with fewer than three competitors, threatening future monopoly pricing on off-patent insulins [S2].

An expedited FDA review pathway for biosimilars of insulin products with inadequate competition lowers their cost and time to market; their gains come from price competition that would lower what patients and plans pay [S2].

ERISA plans are covered by the mandate, so large employers would pick up the tab for deductible-free, capped insulin coverage for employees who use insulin, offset by healthier workforces and avoided catastrophic diabetes complications [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With less than four months left in this Congress and no markup scheduled in any of the three committees of referral, the likely path is that the bill expires in committee without a vote when the session ends in January 2027, and would have to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress.
